full_judgment:
2. The appellant as petitioner filed an application under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 being Misc. Case No. 116 of 1982 before the Subordinate Judge, Sirajganj for pre-emption of two decimals of land. The respondent No. 1 opposed the said petition by filing a written objection. The appellant examined 4 P. Ws. In support of his case whereas the respondent No. 1 examined one witness in support of her case. The learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and order dated 27.6.86 allowed the pre-emption case. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order the respondent No. 1 preferred Misc. Appeal No. 51 of 1985. The learned District Judge, Sirajgonj by his judgment and order dated 24.8.88 dismissed the appeal. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid decision of the court of appeal below the respondent No. 1 as petitioner filed Civil Revision No. 492 of 1986 before the High Court Division, who by its judgment and order dated 29.7.93 made the Rule absolute. 

 5. There is no doubt that under Mohamadan Law there must be an offer, acceptance and delivery of possession of the property thought to be gifted to constitute valid gift. Let us examine as to whether the mother of the respondent No. 1 had made the valid gift of the land in favour of her daughter, the respondent No.1. It appears that in support of the gift the husband of the donor as S. W.1 has categorically stated in chief as well as in cross that the mother of the respondent No.1 had gifted 1(one) decimal of land in favour of her daughter, and she (respondent   No.1) accepted the offer, and the donor had delivered possession of the land. Therefore, the respondent No.1 became the co-sharer, otherwise than by purchase. Therefore, in view of section 24(11) (a) of the Act, 1949 the pre-emption is not available; in fact the pre-emption is barred under section 24(II) (a) of the Non-Agricultural   Tenancy Act, 1949, which provides that nothing in this section shall apply to a transfer made to a co-sharer in the Tenancy whose existing interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase. It appears that the disputed transfer was, by Heba and not by purchase. Therefore, the prayer of the appellant must fail. The pre-emptor appellant failed to prove that the Heba deed was not acted upon. Both the courts below namely, trial court as well as appellate court have wrongly found that the Heba was not completed inasmuch as no possession was delivered to the Donee (the respondent No.1). This finding of fact though concurrent but it is contrary to evidence on record; the perusal of evidence of D.W.1 will shown that the gift was validly made, and the respondent No.1 became the co-sharer of land otherwise than by purchase and the courts bellow illegally allowed the pre-emption at the instance of the appellant. The High Court Division thought made the Rule absolute but the High Court Division went to a wrong premises inasmuch as that the pre-emption proceeding in the instant case shall fail as the pre-emption was sought for a partition of the holding but the conclusion of the High Court Division is correct inasmuch as the pre-emptee is a co-sharer in the holding otherwise than by purchase; Heba though is a transfer but not a transfer by purchase and transfer of a portion of the holding in such manner is protected and pre-emption for such transfer does not lie against such transferee. Pre-emption in case of such transfer by Heba is barred under section 24(11) (a) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. 

 6. Considering the facts and circumstance of the case we are of the view that the appellant has failed to prove although that the Heba was not acted upon and/or that the Heba was not complete. Heba was valid as the requirement of Heba was fully complied with. Therefore, we have no hesitation to hold that the pre-emtee became the co-sharer in holding otherwise than by purchase, and preemption is not maintainable against her and the appeal must fail.
